name: Jason Nitti
about: Jason Nitti’s career began in early 2000 as a music producer in the Atlanta scene. His avant garde approach to music and marketing attracted attention from such industry greats as Dr. Dre, Jimmy Iovine and Timbaland. But Jason found he could offer more than just beats to local music acts. He saw the opportunity for branding in a crowded local hip hop scene. Jason’s aptitude for marketing and design would later land him in the New York City advertising world. He naturally gravitated towards brands looking to leverage non-traditional approaches to advertising. This meant staying on top of the latest technological and digital innovations in a landscape vying for cultural relevancy.

Jason is an award-winning creative where he’s managed and led multi-disciplined creative departments at agencies like Anomaly, 72&Sunny, KidinaKorner and Huge. He recently developed the story practice at Atlanta’s Goods & Services where he helped evolve it into a full service creative shop.

From creating a first ever Oculus VR collaboration between industry giants, Marvel and Samsung to collaborating with IBM’s Watson and Alex Da Kid to help make a hit song, Jason is always welcome to new challenges and landscapes. He’s led fully integrated projects spanning traditional media, experience design, TV, social and experiential for many of the world’s forward-thinking brands.

projects.title: We Are Living in a Stimulation
projects.summary:
I’ve spent most of my career inside creative systems — agencies, music, technology — and I kept noticing the same thing.

For some people, creativity isn’t inspiration. It’s compulsion.

This book isn’t about productivity or finding your muse. It’s an attempt to name the pattern behind creative compulsion, the cycle many of us live inside without realizing it.

I wrote it mostly to understand myself. If it helps someone else feel a little less alone in the process, that’s enough.

details.label: Project type
details.text: Published Book — Kool Head Press, Atlanta

details.label: Framework
details.text: The Echo Cycle: ⌁ Breach ⇌ Glitch ↻ Drift ⇒ Unleash

items.title: The Book
items.caption: One part memoir, one part reframe. Not a book about finding your muse — a field guide for the people who don’t get inspired so much as infected: the bridge that cracks your ribs, the stranger’s laugh that becomes a protagonist, the lights still on at 2:17 AM. It names the pattern so the compulsion stops looking like chaos.

items.title: The Type System
items.caption: Two voices, two typefaces. OCR-B — drawn in 1968 for machines to read — speaks as the Stimulation: chapter marks, diagnostics, the system addressing you. Freight Text Pro carries the human testimony underneath it. No ornament, no pull-quote theatrics; the argument is the tension between the two, set in type and left alone.

items.title: The Echo Cycle
items.caption: The book’s core model, drawn as signal: ⌁ Breach, ⇌ Glitch, ↻ Drift, ⇒ Unleash. Each phase owns a glyph, and the glyphs recur through the interior as wayfinding — a notation system the reader learns the same way the author did: by repetition.

items.title: Transmission
items.caption: The book trailer — an excerpt from the chapter of the same name. Cut to transmit the book’s worldview rather than summarize it. Sound on.

projects.title: IEX - Stock Exchange
projects.summary: When industry competitors publicly questioned IEX’s “most liquidity” claim and suggested they were too small to make an impact anyway, IEX needed creative solutions to refute and debunk these challenges and raise brand awareness.

details.label: Output
details.text: Online Videos, OOH, Social, Campaign, Naming, Brand Identity, Package Design, Influencer kits

items.title: The Challenge
items.caption:
Brad Katsuyama, recognizing the stock market's exploitation by predatory traders, founded IEX with a vision to democratize trading fairness for all Americans. His disruptive approach, aimed at correcting market abuses, earned significant attention, including a feature in Michael Lewis's NY Times bestseller "Flash Boys" and an upcoming Netflix movie, despite stirring controversy on Wall Street.

One way IEX planned to achieve their goal of leveling the financial playing field was to provide the “best liquidity” in the industry, or, in simpler terms, make it easier—and therefore more profitable—for brokers to trade stocks.

items.title: Liquidity. Literally.
items.caption:
Early on, we realized something: if there’s anything stock traders love more than money, it’s beer. So we gathered a group of brokers together, held a beer tasting, and brewed their favorite.

Introducing Liquidity from IEX. The official, unofficial beer of the stock market.

To actually make Liquidity beer come to life, we had some heavy lifting to do. We needed a name, a brand, a style of beer, a complete packaging system, and a roll out strategy.

items.title: Hijacking the Moment
items.caption:
We have a beer. Let’s make some beer ads.

#StockUpResponsibly

We brewed, designed, and distributed a signature IPA and unveiled it during advertising's biggest moment — the super bowl….directing attention to IEX’s goal to help level the playing field.

items.title: Cheers
items.caption:
Everyone knows traditional email campaigns are boring. 

Introducing Liquidity beer was a clever way to literally put that liquidity into people’s hands. 

We gifted Liquidity beer to key clients and launched a social media promotion.

We collaborated with Good Word Brewing for production, including special editions.

items.title: Case Study
items.caption: Making a beer wasn’t just a fun way to get people to the party, it also acted as a conversation starter that led to dynamic, in-person discussions with key players in the industry about IEX and the validity of their “best liquidity” position.

items.title: Results
items.caption:
IEX experienced a considerable measurable uptick in both qualitative and quantitative areas. IEX’s main goals were to raise awareness and increase positive sentiment toward the company, and, as their marketing team said, this campaign accomplished both of those in new and surprising ways.

On the media side, the Liquidity beer story was covered by Adweek in a series of articles. And, as a data point, in 2019, before the campaign, IEX it was trading stocks valued at $10 billion a day. After the Liquidity campaign that’s up to $20 billion a day.

projects.title: High Desert Cactus Vodka
projects.summary: High Desert is a Austin based vodka brand that was created authentically from the ground up. Everything about the story is true and accurate by design. No part of it was manufactured or staged, keeping it simple, iconic, honest, and most of all, competitive.

items.title: In the Making
items.caption:
Inspired by the beauty and bounty of the Southwest, founders Logan Sligar and Ryan Springer wanted to make a spirit out of the prickly pear cactus fruit. A new kind of vodka brand was born.

Creating a new brand of vodka presents a myriad challenges For one thing, High Desert was based in Austin where both Titos and Deep Eddy’s had carved out strong allegiances with customers and distributors.

However High Desert had a handful of key advantages that set them apart. For one thing, as the new flavor on the block they were fresh, different, a new jolt to the vodka space. For another the cactus element gave them a unique aspect that allowed them to straddle both the vodka and tequila markets. For another the prickly pear, and the method of farming they employed, proved to be highly sustainable so their story included the angle of a renewable resource.

items.title: The Ask
items.caption:
Build the High Desert brand from the ground up in a way that celebrates the product's heritage and hand-made spirit and differentiates it from everything else on the shelf.

So we took a trip to the source: San Luis Potosi, Mexico

items.title: Vision and Voice
items.caption: Our trip to the source provided a wealth of assets for our campaign.

items.title: In the Making
items.caption: We even hand carved a cactus for the bottle label keeping in line the "In the Making" brand positioning.

items.title: Design with Spirit
items.caption: Even the label alluded the mountain vistas of San Luis Potosi, with the hand torn front and back label to create depth.

items.title: Live There
items.caption:
When you stay in an Airbnb you feel like you live there. And not just in the house. In that neighborhood. In that town. That cool coffee shop on the corner is YOUR cool coffee shop. That neighbor is your neighbor. Staying in an Airbnb doesn't feel like staying. It feels like living. 

At a global launch event, Airbnb’s uncompromising CEO Brian Chesky championed ‘Live There’ as a tenet of the brand’s future.

items.title: Objective
items.caption: Airbnb, the global online marketplace for lodging and travel experiences, aimed to redefine travel and encourage users to experience destinations like a local. The #LiveThere campaign sought to promote the idea of authentic and unique travel experiences facilitated by Airbnb, emphasizing a departure from traditional tourist experiences.

items.title: Reinforced Brand Positioning
items.caption: The global campaign features :15, :30 and :60 second TV spots, as well as digital, out-of-home, and print. Additionally, disruptive, bespoke social activations drive added engagement on Pinterest, Facebook, Twitter and Snapchat.

items.title: Results
items.caption: Faced with wining over the cool kids with declining awareness growth, Airbnb had to reach beyond its millennial core to a broader audience. By directly challenging how they were traveling, Dont Go There. Live There became the most successful campaign in Airbnbs history

items.title: Love This? Live there.
items.caption:
As a sister promo, we told travelers if they can dream it. They can live it.



45 million international tourists chose a travel destination just because they saw a movie or TV show that was filmed there. And who can blame them? With castles and cabins, treehouses and private islands, you really can live in the movies you love with Airbnb.

projects.title: Rheem Water Heaters
projects.summary: Everyone in the industry already knew that Rheem had been a trusted leader in the water heating space for nearly 100 years. They thought it was time the public knew it, too.

details.label: Output
details.text: Broadcast TVC, Streaming Pre-Roll, Social, Digital, Landing Page refresh

items.title: Comfort Since 1925 and Counting
items.caption:
Rheem is a company that has been a leader in the water heating and air conditioning business for more than 100 years. And while most consumers may not be familiar with the name, contractors, plumbers, and others players in the trade were well aware that Rheem was one of the top go to brands in the space.

In a post COVID world, hot water usage was going up and emerging companies like GE and LG saw an opportunity to seriously compete in the water heater market. Both brands were already household names to consumers, unlike Rheem.

So Rheem decided it was time to turn up the heat, so to speak, and came and was looking to create their first consumer facing ad campaign in more than 50 years.

items.title: Meet the Robinsons
items.caption:
We wanted to create a scenario where Rheem became a comforting presence in a family’s life, where family life and culture could be the hero. Almost like the water heater was a character in their story, even a member of their family.

We borrowed from popular shows like Modern Family and the office which use humorous, one-on-one, documentary style filmmaking. “The Robinson Family” became a consistent narrative device and ambassador for the brand. It’s our Progressive Insurance’s “Flo” or “Jake” from State Farm.

items.title: Family Tie-Ins
items.caption: The benefits of creating a family tie in were abundant. Because each video focused primarily on one member of the Robinsons, it gave us five very different interesting character paths to explore, all with their own evolving lives and personalities, that were rich for social media content. You could follow the daughter’s ever changing passions for years to come.

items.title: Living the Stream
items.caption:
The ads ran on streaming channels including Hulu, Roku, Sling TV, and others, as well as on the streaming feed of “This Old House,” and on the web feeds of networks like AMC, CBS, NBC, Bravo, and USA, among others. Additionally, digital display ads, including GIF banners, and social media platforms run on YouTube, Facebook, Twitter and Instagram.

For this reason we made sure that the spots we created echoed, and were relevant to, the content on the channels they lived on.

items.title: Campaign with Character
items.caption: The episodic nature of the spots also allowed us an element of longevity and durability. If we were asked to do another campaign, we could always check in with the Robinsons to see how they were getting on in life. After all, no matter how old you are, you always need a dependable water heater.

items.title: A Home In-House
items.caption: We wrote, shot, directed, photographed, and produced all in house. The  episodic, sitcom style campaign featuring the Robinsons, allowed us to also share snippets of relatable everyday experiences and how differently they used hot water.

items.title: Rheem, Behind the Steam
items.caption: We had such great character actors, we decided to get some extra social content in between takes. We set up a Rheem branded red seamless for behind the scene interviews with our family. This allowed a deeper connection to the characters, but also relatable family anecdotes and banter with the water heater central to a comfortable family life.

projects.title: SoftShox
projects.summary:
SoftShox builds soft helmet technology — Stanford bioengineering designed to absorb the impacts hard shells can’t. Founded by former athletes who turned their own concussions into the mission, they needed what every product company wants: their swoosh.

The answer was already in their old wordmark. Duplicate the S, flip it, and the overlap draws a single S in the negative space — SoftShox spelled in one gesture instead of ten letters. The two abstract forms do double duty: they’re also a pair of shock absorbers, which is the whole point of what the company engineers.

details.label: Output
details.text: Logo mark, wordmark lockups, color system, product & apparel applications

items.title: The Mark
items.caption: The reveal. One mark, two S’s, no box — bold enough to read at chin-strap size, quiet enough to sit on black. Protection, fluidity, precision, in a single shape.

items.title: From the Old Mark
items.caption: I started with what they had: a boxed wordmark, SOFT stacked over SHOX — safe, forgettable, no mark to speak of. Duplicate the S, flip it, and let the two overlap. Where they cross, the negative space draws a single S — SoftShox said in one gesture instead of two words. The pair of forms is also a small piece of engineering logic: two abstract shocks, absorbing side by side, exactly like the product.

items.title: The System
items.caption: Lockups and inversions: black, white, and the electric blue accent. SOFTSHOX sets in quiet spaced caps beneath the icon — restrained type, so the mark does the talking.

items.title: Engineered In
items.caption: The mark isn’t bolted onto the product after the fact — it’s drafted into the shell itself. Set inside the actual CAD model, the S sits where the engineering lives, proof the identity and the bioengineering share one language.

items.title: Embossed
items.caption: Inside the helmet, not on it. Debossed into the padding the mark works in the one place a swoosh usually doesn’t bother going — where the product actually meets the head.

items.title: On Body
items.caption: The merch test — cap, hoodie, tee. If people would wear it without knowing what the company does, it’s a logo. If it still reads as flow from ten feet, it’s a brand.

Ecolab, a global leader in water, hygiene, and energy technologies, is committed to creating a cleaner, safer, and healthier world. Their partnership with ProStart showcases this mission by empowering the next generation of culinary talent.

The film debuted at an unforgettable gala, where guests experienced the students' winning dishes firsthand at a pop-up restaurant designed and curated entirely by the students—an inspiring blend of mentorship, tradition, and innovation.

projects.title: Cart.com
projects.summary: Cart.com wanted to work with companies they thought were cool and progressive, so we captured a voice that would tap into the language of modern culture to appeal to these types of brands

items.title: Challenge
items.caption: Cart.com is a new digital marketing platform making a big noise in the ecommerce world. To help them build awareness, we created the “Dearest” campaign, an affectionate — some might even say obsessive — expression of love that puts the “court order” back into “courtship.”

items.title: Courting brands
items.caption:
Our concept of publicly posting love letters to the company’s favorite brands pairs old-school signage with the stopping power of a public social post. The campaign is called “Dearest” and it turns B2B marketing on its head. We likened it to serenading a sweetheart beneath a bedroom window – but with an edge.

The poster-sized love letters are visible in major cities like LA, San Francisco, Austin, and Atlanta, and include 36 different brands, such as Liquid Death, BeautyCounter, and Toms. The passionate side of our brand voice describes the lengths that Cart.com will go to help a brand – if they commit to a relationship.
Targeted brands also receive a care package that keeps the love alive and carries the same brand voice throughout.

items.title: Case Study
items.caption:
Employing a barrage of (very) personally targeted, fun, irreverent, and tongue-in-cheek love letters, we helped Cart.com fervently express the depths and breadths of its affection and commitment. Cart then printed each letter as oversized posters and placed them, guerilla style, in heavily trafficked areas of Austin, Los Angeles, and around the country for the world to bear witness to Cart’s undying devotion.

And because Cart wanted everyone to know how excited they were about their crushes, the team posted about our love letters on LinkedIn (#dearest) so the whole world could know. After all, the Cart wants what the Cart wants.

projects.title: Time Hopper
projects.summary: There are travel influencers, and then there’s the first time-traveling one, born from the unapologetic power of A.I.

items.title: Meet Time Hopper
items.caption: Time Hopper is Sparkloft Media’s unapologetically A.I. travel influencer. A time-hopping rabbit who explores the past and future to make history trend again. Instead of blurring the line between human and synthetic, Hopper embraces his artificial identity to show how destinations can use A.I. responsibly, creatively, and transparently. Blending humor, cultural insight, and historical storytelling, the project redefines influencer marketing for the post-human era, a proof-of-concept where technology becomes a collaborator, not an impostor, and authenticity comes from intention, not illusion.

projects.title: Heavily vs Ryan Whitby
projects.summary: Music + Code Project

items.title: Off-Scripted
items.caption:
Heavily is a music project by Jason Nitti. 

The world of Heavily is not just sonic, but highly visual, making it vital for Nitti to integrate artistic elements by showcasing visual artists to help bring the album to life.

Nitti collaborated with artist/designer Ryan Whitby, who created these animations with code inside the visual development platform Touchdesigner.  By scripting behaviors rather than keyframes the pieces naturally respond to the music of Heavily in an almost sentient manner.

items.title: In Ryan's Words...
items.caption: "The animated artwork for Heavily was born from a daily meditative practice during the New York lockdown in 2020.  The animations are largely inspired by the incessant passage of time and the void in which our memories live.  They are the imperfect recollections of a world outside, behind, and yet to come. Platonic shapes, lunar images, point cloud scans of renaissance statues, and AI-generated video of fictional landscapes, are used as varied source material for each animation to be distorted and reconstructed as a sampling of the fevered dream of reality."

items.title: What is Stereo Melon?
items.caption:
Stereo Melon was born from hanging out with my newborn daughter, Sloane. Telling her stories I made up on the go unleashed a wave of creativity and motivation to bring these stories to life.

Stereo Melon has become a growing collection of vibrant characters, magical landscapes, and endless adventures. 

The music is also composed by me, carefully crafted with soothing solfeggio frequencies tuned to promote relaxation, healing, and overall well-being.

Continue to watch some stories!

items.title: A.I. Assisted Content
items.caption: A.I. is a thing right now, and I fully embrace its potential to help bring ideas to life while streamlining the process. I’ve found there's a perfect mixture of right and left brain thinking when it comes to prompting and execution with A.I. I’ve captured my creative process along the way and plan on sharing all the quirks, pivots, adaptation and happy accidents along the way.
